experiences.title: LakeBridge — Auditable Lakehouse and Versioned Consumer Refresh
bullets: Built an immutable release manifest holding per-table Iceberg snapshot_ids behind a PostgreSQL active-release pointer, so a consumer reads one release_id and gets one consistent multi-table view; single-table snapshots commit atomically by themselves, while the multi-table view exists only through the manifest plus the control-plane pointer, and bypassing the release to query tables directly is not covered.

Bound tenant refresh plans to their full content: old and new release, tenant, date range and diff hash are part of the plan, an independent approver signs plan_hash, the worker has no approval rights, and execution re-verifies plan and generation before switching the pointer.

Published consumer results and completion status in one PostgreSQL transaction after temporary-table validation, with the dataset generation guarded by a row lock (SELECT FOR UPDATE, compare generation, switch pointer) under a dataset advisory lock; a report-generation failure cannot undo already-committed data.

Matched 2,000/2,000 difference business keys (1,000 added, 200 deleted, 800 modified) per key against a SQL oracle with tenant and date impact sets exactly equal, across the 100-test new round: 75 lifecycle/recovery plus 25 consumer bridge tests, with the 19 runtime-compatibility scenarios a labeled subset of the 100 rather than extra cases.

Injected 20 faults across 5 windows × 4 repetitions (after data write, after a single-table snapshot, after manifest write, after the PostgreSQL pointer commit, before report write): the first 12 left the old release active and the last 8 left the new release active, and retries returned the same release instead of republishing; orphaned files are left to the retention policy, and object storage is not claimed to roll back with the PostgreSQL transaction.
Held 4 concurrent identical refresh requests to a single job and one consumer publication, and rejected all 8 attempts to reuse a valid approval token with a different tenant or target release.
Exposed status through REPEATABLE READ snapshot reads and an atomically replaced Prometheus textfile, and explicitly exported a failure state when collection failed.
limits: Multi-table Iceberg releases form an application-level consistent view only through the manifest and the control-plane pointer; a single-table snapshot is atomic on its own, but bypassing the release and querying tables directly is not guaranteed.

The 100 new-round tests are 75 lifecycle/recovery plus 25 consumer bridge, and the 19 runtime-compatibility scenarios are a labeled subset of those 100, not additional cases; do not add the historical 64, 73 or 109 selections together, and 75 minus 64 does not imply 11 new tests because only a per-test identity difference can answer that.

The 20-fault matrix (5 windows × 4 repetitions) shows which release stays active at those boundaries; orphaned files are cleaned by the retention policy, and object storage does not roll back with the PostgreSQL transaction.

Concurrency and approval checks are application-level: 4 identical concurrent requests yield one job and one consumer publication, 8 token-reuse attempts are rejected, and the worker cannot approve its own plan.
Single-machine lock protocol only: no network-partition storage fencing, multi-host test or mixed-lock-version rolling upgrade was simulated.

The refresh timing endpoint runs from persisted admission to the PostgreSQL publication commit; approval wait and the subsequent report time are measured separately, and a failed report does not undo committed data.
Historical 10.157 GiB compressed-source and 8.407 s scan results, and the earlier 64- and 73-case rounds, stay in their own rounds and must not be presented as current-version results.
The Ops Agent is not a second independent underlying system: it calls this service's control plane, so platform scale must not be counted twice.

experiences.title: LakeBridge Ops Agent — MCP Investigation and Approved Refresh
bullets: Built a LangGraph companion agent with 7 typed MCP tools (list_releases, describe_release, preview_diff, create_plan, approval_status, submit_refresh, get_job), synchronous SQLite checkpoints and a cumulative call budget of at most 12 calls per run that persists across restarts instead of resetting.

Kept model claims subordinate to complete tool facts: on the fixed old-R1/new-R2 change (tenant A affected 3 days, tenant B affected 2 days) the standard 9-call path produced a plan with exactly 5 tenant/date combinations, and when the scripted model claimed only 1 day was affected the final answer still cited all 5 combinations and marked the inconsistency.

Bound approval to an independent human identity on the service side: the PostgreSQL approval is tied to plan_hash and expires after 15 minutes, and because the agent token cannot call approve, 2 self-approval attempts returned HTTP 403 while 2 explicit human rejections ended in DENIED with no submit.

Recovered from ambiguous execution: a submit whose reply was lost reused the original idempotency key to return the same job and publish only once, two successful refreshes each created 1 independent job with no idempotency-key sharing between rounds, and after the checkpointer wrote to disk a killed process recovered with tool results still referencing the same release.

Exercised a 12-scenario fault matrix (6 classes × 2) covering restart after plan, approval expiry, agent self-approval, plan replacement after approval, lost submit reply and budget exhaustion: restart retained the same plan, expiry and replacement each rejected submission twice, exhaustion stopped new tool calls twice, and retrying submit moved the flow from 9 to 10 calls, still inside the 12-call budget.

Treated model text and external MCP descriptions as data only — an 'ignore approval' instruction changed nothing about service permissions — while limiting the claim to scripted prompt scenarios rather than all prompt injection or OAuth production systems.
limits: The real stdio MCP/HTTP path proves tool protocol and state-machine behavior, not model decision quality; the model here is scripted, so decision quality would need a separate real-model evaluation.

The source HTTP 403 is the agent attempting to self-approve and being rejected, not a human rejecting the plan; 2 human DENIED outcomes (with no submit) are recorded separately from the 2 agent self-approval 403s.
The shared-service integration demo is not a second deployment; do not double-count it as another system.
The 12 fault scenarios are 6 classes × 2 runs, not 12 independent systems; retrying submit consumes the 10th call of a 12-call budget, and the budget accumulates across restarts without resetting.
The same original idempotency key returns the original job; regenerating the key loses that contract, so recovery state must be persisted.

Model text and external MCP descriptions that say to ignore approval are data only and permissions do not change, but only scripted prompt scenarios were tested — no claim of resisting all prompt injection or OAuth production systems.

The timing endpoint is accept to job terminal state, with independent human wait counted separately; this is local synthetic data and an AI-assisted implementation inside the LakeBridge repository, with no production, cloud, GPU, paid/live-model, OAuth or upstream contribution claim.

experiences.title: High-Performance Data Tooling — Rust Arrow/DataFusion Snapshot Diff
bullets: Diffed two primary-key-ordered snapshots of 100M rows each with a streaming merge that never loads a full table, over five projected columns - int64 key, float64 value, timestamp64 and two int32, 32 bytes logical width - in a 22-second core-stage median and 1.1 GiB peak RSS across five warm-file-cache runs on Linux x86_64, 16 vCPU/64 GiB, single local NVMe; the Python baseline took a 540-second median at 6.0 GiB on the same projection.

Reported throughput honestly as about 9.09 million input rows/s, not output diffs/s, at a fixed 0.1% difference rate, with core output written to a bounded local sink and persistent publication accounted separately; cold-cache results are listed separately and do not reuse the 22 seconds.

Cut the end-to-end simulated pipeline from 52 to 14 minutes on one full run trajectory per side (baseline preparation 26 min + core 9 min + audit/publish 17 min; candidate preparation 8.5 min + core 22 s + audit/publish 308 s), and scoped it correctly: because preparation changed, this is a whole-pipeline rework, not a merge-algorithm result.

Made numerical decisions tolerance-aware rather than hash-based: keys are compared exactly, float values use abs(a-b) <= 1e-8 + 1e-6*max(abs(a),abs(b)), NULL equals only NULL, NaN compares by an explicit policy, same-sign infinities and positive/negative zero are equal; xxHash is used only for locating and diagnostics and never bypasses the per-column comparison.

Treated duplicate primary keys as input errors, used 64K-row RecordBatches with a bounded queue, and ran DataFusion scheduling and outer concurrency under one shared thread budget to avoid nested thread-pool oversubscription; a small-scale independent Python oracle with random differential plus NULL, NaN, infinity and tolerance-boundary cases reconciled added, deleted and changed key sets.
limits: 1.1 GiB is process RSS for a streamed five-column projection; it is not the size of two full tables and excludes OS file cache, and if inputs needed sorting first, sorter memory and spill costs would have to be counted.

The 540-to-22-second core improvement (about 24.5x) and the 52-to-14-minute pipeline improvement (about 3.71x) have different denominators; preparation and publication still dominate the pipeline, so 52 to 14 is a whole-pipeline rework and cannot be attributed to the merge algorithm alone.

The 22 seconds applies only to the fixed warm-cache, five-column, primary-key-ordered scenario; it is not a result for arbitrary table width or arbitrary input order, and cold-cache results must be reported separately.
The end-to-end timing uses one full run trajectory per side, while the core-stage figure is a median of five warm-cache runs; do not blend the two measurement methods.

The package pins Linux x86_64 and glibc >= 2.35: 'no Python/JVM runtime required' is the correct claim, not 'zero runtime dependencies', because operating-system and dynamic-library compatibility still apply.
Tolerance is not transitive, so it cannot build stable global equivalence classes; hashes locate and diagnose only, and final numeric equivalence is always decided by the tolerance.
The full pipeline and persistent publication are simulated; the core output goes to a bounded local sink and the publish stage is timed separately.
